questions.question: A 10 by 10 grid is made of 100 equal small squares, and the whole grid stands for 100%. Kiran shades 46 of the small squares blue. What percent of the grid is shaded?
questions.explain: The grid has 100 equal parts, so each small square is 1 part per hundred, or 1%; 46 shaded squares means 46 out of 100, which is 46%. The usual trap is answering 54%, which counts the squares that are left unshaded.

questions.question: A 10 by 10 grid is made of 100 equal small squares, and the whole grid stands for 100%. Sofia shades 62 small squares and leaves the rest white. What percent of the grid is NOT shaded?
questions.explain: All 100 equal parts together are 100%, so the white part is 100 - 62 = 38 parts per hundred, which is 38%. Many students stop at 62% because that is the number given in the question, but that is the shaded part.

questions.question: On a 10 by 10 grid of 100 equal small squares, Ravi shades 25 squares. He says ‘That is 25% of the grid.’ Which sentence best explains why Ravi is correct?
options: Because the word percent just means the number you shade, so shading 25 squares is 25% of anything.
Because each small square on this grid is worth one tenth, so 25 squares is 25%.
Because the grid has 100 equal parts and percent means parts per hundred, so 25 shaded parts is 25%.
Because 25 is smaller than 100, and any number smaller than 100 can be written with a % sign.
questions.explain: Percent means ‘per hundred’, so a 10 by 10 grid works because it is split into exactly 100 equal parts and each part is 1%. Watch out for the idea that a percent is just a plain count — 25% only equals 25 things when the whole is 100 things.

questions.question: A 10 by 10 grid has 100 equal small squares arranged in 10 rows of 10. Emily shades exactly one whole row, which is one tenth of the whole grid. What percent of the grid is shaded?
questions.explain: One row holds 10 of the 100 equal squares, so that is 10 parts per hundred, or 10%; one tenth and 10 hundredths are the same amount. The common slip is saying 1% because only one row was shaded — count the small squares, not the rows.

questions.question: Emma scored 84 out of 100 on a math quiz at her Kamloops school. Which statement writes her score as a percent AND explains it correctly?
options: 84%, because 84 out of 100 equal parts is 84 parts per hundred.
8.4%, because 84 out of 100 is the same as 84 tenths.
16%, because a percent always tells you the part that is missing.
84, because a percent is just the score itself and the % sign does not change anything.
questions.explain: A score out of 100 is already parts per hundred, so 84 out of 100 is 84%. The trap is treating a percent as a plain number: 84% is a comparison to a whole of 100, not simply the number 84.

questions.question: Leo says, ‘7% and 7 tenths are the same amount.’ Which statement is correct?
options: Leo is right, because 7% and 7 tenths both stand for the number 7.
Leo is wrong: 7% is 7 hundredths, but 7 tenths is 70 hundredths, so 7 tenths is much bigger.
Leo is wrong: 7% is 70 hundredths, so 7% is the bigger amount.
Leo is wrong: 7% means 7 out of 10, so 7% is the bigger amount.
questions.explain: Percent means hundredths, so 7% is 7 small squares of a 100-square grid, while 7 tenths is 7 whole rows, which is 70 of those squares. The trap is reading the digit 7 in both and assuming they match — always check whether the parts are tenths or hundredths.

questions.question: A 10 by 10 grid of 100 equal squares is used to show a whole bag of 200 marbles, so each small square stands for 2 marbles. Nadia shades 30 squares, which is 30% of the bag. How many marbles does the shaded part stand for?
options: 30 marbles
3 marbles
60 marbles
170 marbles
questions.explain: 30% means 30 out of every 100 equal parts, and here each part is 2 marbles, so 30 parts is 30 x 2 = 60 marbles. The big trap is answering 30 marbles — a percent is not a count on its own, its size depends on how big the whole is.

questions.question: Which line gives three ways of writing 60% that are all correct?
options: 60 out of 10, 6.0, and 6 wholes
6 out of 100, 0.06, and 6 hundredths
the plain number 60, because 60% and 60 always mean the same amount
60 out of 100, 0.60, and 6 tenths
questions.explain: Percent means per hundred, so 60% is 60 of the 100 small squares, which is 0.60, and 60 hundredths is the same as 6 tenths (6 full rows). The trap is dropping the % sign and treating 60% as the plain number 60, which ignores the whole it is being compared to.

questions.question: A hoodie at a Burnaby store costs $40 and the sign says 25% off. Ana says, ‘That saves me $25.’ How much is really saved?
options: $10, because 25% means 25 hundredths of the price, and 25 hundredths of $40 is $10.
$15, because you subtract 25 from the price of $40.
$4, because 25% off is the same as taking one tenth off.
$25 — Ana is right, because 25% off means $25 off any price.
questions.explain: Think of $40 spread over a 100-square grid: each square is 40 cents, so 25 squares is 25 x $0.40 = $10 off, leaving $30 to pay. Ana fell into the most common trap — using 25% as the plain number 25 instead of 25 parts out of every 100 of the price.

questions.question: A board game costs $60 at a Richmond store and is marked 10% off. Imagine the full price spread over a 10 by 10 grid, so the whole grid is $60. What do you actually pay?
options: $50, because 10% off means you take away 10
$54, because 10% is 10 hundredths of $60, which is $6 off
$6, because 10% of $60 is $6, and that is the price you pay
$66, because the 10% is added to the price
questions.explain: Each small square of the grid is $0.60, so 10 squares (10%) is $6 off, and $60 - $6 = $54 to pay. Two traps live here: taking away a plain 10, and stopping at the discount ($6) instead of the price you hand over.

questions.question: Liam shades 30 squares on a 10 by 10 grid of 100 equal squares and says, ‘That is 30%, so 30% of my 50 stickers must be 30 stickers.’ Which answer corrects him?
options: He is right — 30% always means 30 things.
20 stickers, because you take 30 away from the 50 stickers.
15 stickers, because 30% is 30 out of every 100, and 50 is half of 100, so it is half of 30.
5 stickers, because 30% means 30 out of 100, so you divide 50 by 10.
questions.explain: On the grid the whole is 100 squares, so 30% is 30 squares; but with only 50 stickers each ‘square’ is worth half a sticker, giving 15. The misconception to avoid is thinking 30% is fixed at 30 items — the same percent gives different amounts when the whole changes.

questions.question: A tablet costs $200. A shop in Abbotsford takes 50% off it, while an online store takes $50 off the same $200 tablet. Which deal saves more, and why?
options: They are exactly the same deal, because 50% means $50.
The online store, because a dollar amount is always more than a percent.
The Abbotsford shop, because 50% off means you only pay $50.
The Abbotsford shop, because 50% means 50 out of every 100 — that is $100 off, which beats $50 off.
questions.explain: Split $200 into 100 equal parts of $2 each; 50 of those parts is 50 x $2 = $100 off, so you pay $100, while $50 off leaves you paying $150. The trap is matching the digits and thinking 50% and $50 are the same — a percent must always be taken of the whole amount.
